# Results — Study 943 (Reset Frequency) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). We build a **monthly-reset**
replication of 2x and 3x S&P 500 exposure — SPY on margin, financed at **^IRX + 50 bps**,
levered back to target once a month and left to drift in between — and race it against a
**daily-reset** replication and the actual daily-reset funds **SSO** (2x) and **UPRO** (3x).
Every leg is measured **excess-of-cash** (minus BIL's total return). Daily **total-return**
closes (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`) for SPY / SSO / UPRO / BIL; `^IRX` is a **quoted
13-week bill discount yield in percent**, not a price. One execution lag: the reset trade
is decided at the month-end close and is in force from the next session. As-of
**2026-06-30** (the partial current month is dropped).*

**Non-tape inputs, all labelled and swept.** The financing spread over `^IRX` (**50 bps**,
an ASSUMPTION — swept 0→200 bps), the one-way transaction cost on exposure turnover
(**2 bps**, a PROXY — swept 0→10 bps) and the **maintenance-margin ratio** at which a
drifting monthly account is liquidated (**25%**, a Reg-T-flavoured PROXY — swept
0/15/25/30%). The third one is not a detail: at 3x it decides the entire verdict.

**A called account holds cash, not a mattress.** When the maintenance test liquidates an
arm, the proceeds are credited the **cash leg** for the rest of the sample, so a margin
call costs that arm exactly the equity it destroyed on the day and *not* an extra −BIL
drift for the following fifteen years. (Crediting 0% — the natural first draft — cost the
3x monthly arm a spurious −0.07 of excess Sharpe; the invariant is pinned as a unit test.)
A wiped-out account earns nothing, because there is nothing left to deposit.

## Data stamp

| Sleeve | Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2x | SPY, SSO, BIL, ^IRX | 2007-05-31 → 2026-06-30 | 4,799 | `8f71ea1922ec` |
| 3x | SPY, UPRO, BIL, ^IRX | 2009-06-26 → 2026-06-30 | 4,276 | `4a95749c18bb` |

BIL's 2007 inception gates the 2x window; UPRO's 2009 launch gates the 3x one — so the 3x
race never sees 2008 (that gap is filled by the stress run below, whose window is **pinned
at 2004-01-01** rather than inherited from however deep the shared cache happens to go).
**Survivorship:** SSO and UPRO are the two leveraged S&P funds that *survived*; the many
2x/3x products that closed over the period are absent from the tape, which flatters the
daily-reset arm's represented history, not the monthly one.

## 2x sleeve — SSO vs a monthly-reset replication

| Arm | Excess Sharpe | CAGR | Vol | Max drawdown | Terminal | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SSO (the actual 2x fund) | +0.504 | +14.33% | 38.9% | −84.7% | ×12.8 | +2.52 |
| daily-reset replication | +0.527 | +15.45% | 39.6% | −84.2% | ×15.4 | +2.68 |
| **monthly-reset replication** | **+0.549** | **+17.13%** | **42.8%** | **−82.5%** | **×20.3** | +2.95 |
| SPY (1x, reference) | +0.613 | +10.70% | 19.8% | −55.2% | ×6.9 | +3.12 |

- **Monthly − daily: +1.05 bps/day, HAC *t* = +2.79.** The monthly reset really does earn
  more on this tape, and that *t* is on the real tape, not the literature.
- **But the Sharpe advantage is +0.022**, with a paired block-bootstrap CI of
  **[−0.010, +0.062]** (8.7% of resamples negative) — indistinguishable from zero. The
  extra return is bought with extra risk: vol 39.6% → 42.8%, because between resets the
  account's exposure floats (mean **1.998** — the same average leverage as the daily arm —
  min 1.78, **max 3.24** on 2008-10-28). Same average exposure, more return, more vol,
  no Sharpe.
- Monthly-reset bootstrap Sharpe +0.549 [+0.168, +0.951]; daily +0.527 [+0.122, +0.941] —
  two CIs sitting on top of each other.
- **Monthly − SSO: +0.045 of Sharpe.** The HAC *t* = +3.41 that goes with it is on the
  daily **return** difference, not on the Sharpe gap — a higher mean return is what is
  reliably measured; the Sharpe gap has no *t* here, only the bootstrap CI above. Roughly
  half of that +0.045 is not the reset at all: the fund's fee-and-tracking drag
  (daily-synth − SSO) is **+1.21%/yr, HAC *t* = +3.82** on the return difference. That leg
  is not purely a fee, either — it also contains the difference between the fund's real
  borrowing cost and our assumed ^IRX + 50 bps, which is why it shrinks as the spread is
  swept upward (see Robustness, and Study 945 for the funds' implied rate).
- At a 25% maintenance margin the 2x monthly account is **never called** (peak exposure
  3.24 needs a 30.9% equity ratio) — so at 2x the comparison is a fair fight, and the whole
  maintenance sweep is flat.

## 3x sleeve — UPRO vs a monthly-reset replication

| Arm | Excess Sharpe | CAGR | Vol | Max drawdown | Terminal | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| UPRO (the actual 3x fund) | +0.791 | +32.95% | 51.3% | −76.8% | ×125.5 | +3.66 |
| daily-reset replication | +0.808 | +34.17% | 51.3% | −76.2% | ×146.6 | +3.75 |
| **monthly-reset replication** (25% maintenance) | **+0.239** | +4.05% | 18.8% | −48.3% | **×2.0** | +0.93 |
| SPY (1x, reference) | +0.911 | +15.17% | 17.1% | −33.7% | ×11.0 | +4.22 |

- **The 3x monthly-reset account is margin-called on 2011-08-08** (the post-downgrade
  selloff), after exposure drifted to 3.84x. It then holds cash for the following fifteen
  years — earning the cash leg, contributing exactly zero excess return — which is why it
  ends at ×2.0 against the fund's ×125.5 and why its vol reads 18.8%: most of that sample
  is a flat line.
- **Monthly − daily: −14.68 bps/day, HAC *t* = −3.62; Sharpe advantage −0.569**, paired
  bootstrap CI **[−1.085, +0.017]** — 97.1% of resamples negative, but the interval does
  graze zero, so the *size* of the damage is uncertain even though its direction is not.
  Negative in both eras (−0.58, *t* = −2.80 before 2017; −0.56, *t* = −2.48 after).
- **The maintenance-margin PROXY decides this outcome, and we show the whole sweep:**

| Maintenance | Monthly Sharpe | Advantage | Max exposure | Terminal (monthly / daily) | Liquidated |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| 0% (an infinitely patient lender) | +0.812 | **+0.003** | **8.42** | ×227.3 / ×146.6 | never |
| 15% | +0.523 | −0.285 | 5.68 | ×11.2 / ×146.6 | 2020-03-20 |
| **25% (Reg-T-flavoured default)** | +0.239 | **−0.569** | 3.84 | ×2.0 / ×146.6 | 2011-08-08 |
| 30% | +0.373 | +0.124 | 3.30 | ×2.2 / ×2.0 | 2010-05-06 |

  Read the top row carefully: **even with no lender at all**, the 3x monthly reset's
  Sharpe advantage is **+0.003**. It turns a ×146.6 into a ×227.3 on an average exposure of
  **2.98x** — essentially the daily arm's 3.00x — by running vol of **58.5%** against
  51.3% and a drawdown of −82.2% against −76.2%, with a peak exposure of **8.42x** on
  2020-03-24. More money for more risk is not an edge. The 30% row is its own lesson: at
  that requirement even the *daily*-reset margin account is called (2010-05-06, the flash
  crash), which is precisely why these products exist as funds rather than as margin
  accounts — and it is why the +0.124 "advantage" in that row is an artefact of both arms
  being dead, not a win.

## Trending vs choppy — where the gap actually comes from

Per calendar month we regress the reset-frequency gap (monthly minus daily, log, in
percentage points) on the month's **efficiency ratio** ER = |Σ log r| / Σ |log r| on SPY —
1.0 is a straight-line month, ~0 is a month that went nowhere the long way round.

| Sleeve | Slope (pp per unit ER) | HAC *t* | Choppy tercile | Mid | Trending tercile |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2x (229 months) | **−1.250** | −6.83 | **+0.381 pp/mo** (*t* = +4.59) | +0.145 | **−0.164 pp/mo** (*t* = −8.40) |
| 3x (204 months) | **−3.158** | −7.22 | **+0.950 pp/mo** (*t* = +3.91) | +0.186 | **−0.492 pp/mo** (*t* = −8.29) |

The sign is the opposite of the folklore. The daily reset is not the villain: it is the
**hero of trending months** (it compounds a trend; the monthly reset does not) and the
villain only of choppy ones (it rebalances into every reversal). 2007–2026 was, on net,
choppy enough at the daily frequency for the monthly reset to come out marginally ahead.

**This decomposition is arithmetic, not alpha, and the synthetic control proves it:** on an
*iid random walk* the same contemporaneous slope is **−2.29** — because months that
*happened* to be choppy always favour the monthly reset by construction. Only the
unconditional average gap can carry information, and on the null that is +0.03 bps/day
(HAC *t* = +0.27).

**And it is not forecastable.** With the efficiency ratio **lagged one month** the slope
collapses: +0.115 pp (*t* = +0.72) at 2x and +0.659 pp (*t* = +1.61) at 3x. A naive
"use the monthly reset after a choppy month" switch earns +0.060 pp/month (*t* = +2.49) at
2x and +0.041 pp/month (*t* = +1.04) at 3x — a few basis points a month on a 40%-vol
sleeve, and that is with the switch threshold set at the **full-sample** median ER, a
hindsight cut nobody could have used. Treat it as an upper bound, not a backtest.

## Robustness

| Cut | 2x advantage | 3x advantage (25% maintenance) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Full sample | +0.022 (*t* = +2.79) | −0.569 (*t* = −3.62) |
| 2007/09–2016 | +0.047 (*t* = +2.26) | −0.581 (*t* = −2.80) |
| 2017–2026 | +0.004 (*t* = +1.56) | −0.563 (*t* = −2.48) |
| **Era difference (late − early)** | **−0.84 bps/day (*t* = −1.15)** | **−2.37 bps/day (*t* = −0.30)** |
| Financing spread 0 bps | +0.021 (*t* = +2.79) | −0.582 (*t* = −3.70) |
| Financing spread 200 bps | +0.025 (*t* = +2.81) | −0.530 (*t* = −3.36) |
| Cost 0 bps | +0.021 (*t* = +2.73) | −0.572 (*t* = −3.64) |
| Cost 10 bps one-way | +0.029 (*t* = +3.05) | −0.554 (*t* = −3.53) |

Neither sweep moves the answer — the financing spread and the trading cost hit both arms
almost identically, since the two arms hold nearly the same average exposure. The **era**
row needs care, and the house bar forbids reading the two halves as a decay without
testing the difference: the 2x advantage falls from +0.047 to +0.004, but regressing the
daily gap on an era dummy gives **−0.84 bps/day with HAC *t* = −1.15**. The two halves are
*not* statistically distinguishable. The honest reading is that the 2x effect is **not
shown to have decayed** — it is simply never large enough, in either half, to be worth
anything risk-adjusted. The monthly reset's edge over the *fund* (as opposed to over the
daily-reset replication) does erode with financing: +0.056 at a 0 bps spread, +0.010 at
200 bps — that leg is the fee saving, and it is exactly as cheap as your borrowing.

## The 2008 stress the UPRO tape cannot see

UPRO launched in June 2009, so the 3x race above never meets a real bear market. Replaying
the monthly reset on SPY from a pinned **2004-01-01** (5,652 sessions to 2026-06-30, with
`^IRX` accrual as the cash leg, credited to any called account):

| Construction | Terminal | Max drawdown | Peak exposure | Liquidated |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| 2x monthly (25% maintenance) | ×37.6 | −82.5% | 3.24 | never |
| 2x daily | ×27.9 | −84.2% | 2.00 | never |
| 3x monthly, **no lender limit** | ×80.4 | −94.0% | **12.80** | never |
| 3x monthly, 25% maintenance | **×0.96** | −68.2% | 3.95 | **2008-09-29** |
| 3x daily | ×33.8 | −95.5% | 3.00 | never |
| 4x monthly, **no lender limit** | **×0.00** | **−100.0%** | 59.97 | **2008-10-24 (equity gone)** |
| 4x daily | ×17.4 | −99.0% | 4.00 | never |

The 3x monthly account called in September 2008 ends the 22-year run at **×0.96** —
below where it started in 2004, cash accrual included. And the last row is the whole argument
in one line: a daily-reset 4x account cannot go below zero — that is what the daily reset
*buys* you — while a monthly-reset 4x account went to **negative equity** in October 2008.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

Seeds 943–946, an AR(1) choppiness knob at fixed total volatility, liquidation disabled:

| Planted world | Mean gap (monthly − daily) | HAC *t* | Contemporaneous ER slope |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Choppy (φ = −0.15) | **+0.357 bps/day** | +3.74 | −1.99 |
| Trending (φ = +0.15) | **−0.403 bps/day** | −2.47 | −2.65 |
| iid null (φ = 0) | **+0.033 bps/day** | +0.27 | −2.29 |

The detector recovers the planted effect with the right sign in both directions and is
silent on the null — while the ER slope stays strongly negative everywhere, which is the
caveat above, pinned.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Mixed.** *Real on the return, absent on the Sharpe; positive at 2x, negative
  at 3x.* Reset frequency genuinely changes returns, and the direction is real, mechanical
  and well identified: at 2x the monthly reset earned **+1.05 bps/day (HAC *t* = +2.79)**
  over the daily reset on the real tape, and the gap is **positive in choppy months and
  negative in trending ones** in both sleeves (slope *t* = −6.8 / −7.2). But the claim
  under test — that a monthly reset is *better* — fails: the risk-adjusted advantage at 2x
  is **+0.022 with a bootstrap CI of [−0.010, +0.062]**, it is **not forecastable**
  (lagged-ER *t* = +0.72), and at 3x the same construction is **−0.569 (*t* = −3.62)**
  under a standard maintenance margin and only **+0.003** even with an infinitely patient
  lender. Half of what looks like a monthly-reset edge over the funds is simply their
  ~1 pp/yr fee-and-tracking drag. Survivorship is on the daily-reset side of the ledger:
  the leveraged funds that closed are not on this tape.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is no reset-frequency edge to bank. What the monthly
  reset actually delivers is *uncontrolled leverage at the same average leverage*: the same
  ~3.0x mean exposure as the daily arm but with a 8.42x peak, 7 extra points of vol, a
  margin call in 2011 (and in September 2008 on the longer tape), and negative equity
  outright at 4x. The daily reset's supposed vice — pinning exposure every single day — is
  the feature that keeps the position alive, and it costs, on this tape, a statistically
  detectable but economically negligible +0.02 of Sharpe at 2x.
